risks: Privacy and trust: linking health and tenancy data for people who fear enforcement; distress when recounting homelessness; staff feeling judged on referral rates.
consent: Layered consent for interviews (taking part, recording, quotation) explained by the peer researcher, with payment for time; the hospital data comparison uses de-identified records under the approved outline; tenancy linkage only for people who consent or under the terms the ethics board sets once the agreement is signed.
data: No data are shared with police, immigration or benefits agencies; linkage by the provider's named custodian; analysis files hold no names or addresses.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people experiencing homelessness carry disadvantage across place, income, social capital and often disability; women leaving violence, young people leaving care and people from racialised communities may meet different barriers. Interviews purposively include these groups, and results are reported with the community advisory group before release.
effectiveness: The study succeeds if it produces a referral pathway that raises complete referrals and housing within six months.
efficiency: Uses existing staff and data; the peer researcher's time is the main cost.
costs: Peer researcher at 200 hours and participant payments from the inclusion health budget.
grants: None needed for this study; the pathway could later be evaluated with external funding.
partnerships: The housing-first provider, a community advisory group of people with lived experience, the emergency department, and the city's homelessness services.
rebPath: Approved by the research ethics board on 2026-09-01 (REB-2026-188) with the condition that tenancy data wait for a signed data-sharing agreement; the provider's board rejected the first proposal, so that gate is unmet until a revised proposal naming a custodian is accepted.
limitations: Confounding by engagement; interview sample may over-represent people who were housed; two years of referrals from one hospital.
summary: Layered consent, peer-led interviews, strict non-disclosure, and an unmet data-sharing gate.
